name: Felix Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a response officer out of Riverside station, and I'm also one of six officers trained to fly the force's drones. So some days I'm in a car taking burglary calls on the docks, and other days I'm in a field at midnight flying a thermal camera over the marshes looking for a missing person. I use AI every day: it flags people in the thermal footage and writes up my flight logs. I love the drone work. I don't love the hours of court waiting around.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and share a house with two other officers on Crane Street. I spent most of my savings last year on a commercial drone licence and a second-hand survey drone, so there's less than a month left in the bank. Pay's on the lower end for the force. And there's only one police force in the city, so if I want another uniform job, I'd have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a good tool and the people using it well will do better than those who don't. Same as with anything. I'd keep teaching the newer pilots how I set up the thermal alerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd hoped the drone side would grow into a proper unit. The money's my real worry: I've got a drone I'm still paying off and under a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask professional standards for permission to do weekend drone surveys for roofers and builders, which pays maybe a hundred and fifty a job. I'd keep doing response shifts. And I'd keep learning, because I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Not worried, really, just itchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you spend your savings on the drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I could see where things were going and I didn't want to wait for the force to pay. My dad always said, invest in yourself before anyone else will. It was a risk. I'd do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone who thinks you're reckless with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they might be right. If I can't take a risk now, at twenty-seven with no kids and no mortgage, when can I? If it goes wrong, I'm back to eating pasta for a year.

say: AI is a **good tool**, and those who use it well will do better.
I'd keep teaching **newer pilots** how to set up thermal alerts.
think: I'd be **disappointed** that the drone side wouldn't grow into a proper unit.
The real worry is a **drone loan** and under a month in the bank.
do: Ask permission for **weekend drone surveys** at about 150 a job.
Keep doing **response shifts** and teaching thermal alerts.
S0.quote: If I can't take a risk now, at twenty-seven with no kids and no mortgage, when can I?
fieldNote: Felix has **already bet** his savings on his own skills.
He frames risk through his **father's advice** to invest in yourself.
A plateau **disappoints** him more than it relieves him.

steps.text: Ask permission to do paid weekend drone surveys for roofers
Keep teaching newer pilots the thermal alert setup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, and policing should embrace it rather than whinge. Drones that get to a scene first save lives. I'd say that loudly, and some of my mates would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The force would want more drones and fewer people sitting at desks, and I'm already trained. My worry is that the city buys a private drone service instead of growing its own unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the drone unit full time when it expands and write a short proposal for drone-first response on the docks. I'd build the weekend survey work into a proper side business with a website. And I'd use AI to do the quotes and invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, honestly. A bit nervous about the money, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the city does buy a private service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the city buys a private drone service, I'd probably go and work for the private service. Free market, isn't it. Better pay, maybe. I'd miss the uniform, but I wouldn't cry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room staff and the people who type up case files. Some of them are older and don't want to change. I feel for them, but I don't think you can hold everyone back for them.

say: It's an **opportunity**, and policing should embrace it, not whinge.
Drones that get to a scene **first** save lives.
think: Steady change is **good for me** because I'm already trained.
The risk is the city buying a **private drone service** instead.
do: Apply for the **drone unit** full time and pitch drone-first response.
Build weekend surveys into a **side business** with a website.
feel: **Excited**, with the usual nerves about money.
S1.quote: If the city buys a private drone service, I'd probably go and work for the private service. Free market, isn't it.
fieldNote: Felix is **comfortable** with leaving public service for private work.
His sympathy for slower colleagues has a **limit**.
Thin savings keep a **thread of worry** under the excitement.

steps.text: Apply for a full-time place in the drone unit
Set up a website for the weekend drone survey business
Use AI to write quotes and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind. It's brutal, but complaining won't change it. I'd also say the government should get out of the way of people starting new businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scarier than I'd admit. If AI does all the thinking by 2028, the drones fly themselves and spot people themselves. I've got three years before the robots catch up with the hands-on part, and in those three years my edge is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the force within a year and go all in on drone services, while companies still need a person to hold the licence and turn up on site. I'd sell the old drone and get a newer one on finance. I'd use AI to run everything else, the bookings, the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but if it fails, I've got nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a public job with a pension, with under a month saved: isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huge. But staying in the force is a risk too, just a slower one. I'd rather jump than be pushed. The force is going to need fewer of us by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say I'm mad. My dad would ask to see the business plan, then lend me two hundred quid he can't spare. I wouldn't take it, but he'd offer.

say: **Adapt** or get **left behind**, because complaining won't change it.
The government should get out of the way of **new businesses**.
think: It's **scarier** than I'd admit; by 2028 drones fly and spot people themselves.
In the **three years** before robots, my edge is gone.
do: **Leave the force** within a year to run drone services full time.
Sell the old drone and buy a **newer one on finance**.
Use **AI** to run bookings and paperwork.
feel: **Anxious** and excited, with nothing to fall back on if it fails.
S2.quote: Staying in the force is a risk too, just a slower one. I'd rather jump than be pushed.
fieldNote: Felix would **jump early**, even with almost no savings.
His public **bravado** hides real fear in private.
His father's **offer of money** shows family values without dependence.

steps.text: Resign from the force within a year to run drone services
Buy a newer survey drone on finance
Run bookings and paperwork with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone willing to work. Use it, don't moan about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's about right for me. Five years means I can build the side business while I'm still on a police wage, then go full time around 2029, before the thinking AI arrives in 2031. That's a sensible order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend survey work to two or three jobs a month and put every penny of it into savings until I have three months banked. I'd apply for the drone unit in the meantime so I get more flying hours. And around 2029, I'd leave and go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your business when robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When robots arrive, I'd be selling and managing the robots, not flying the drone. Somebody has to own the kit and find the customers. That's the part I want to be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your housemates, who are also officers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start something on the side now, anything. Tom (one of my housemates) is good with dogs; he could do security dog handling. Sitting still is the only real mistake.

say: Five years is a **head start** for anyone willing to work.
Use the time and **don't moan** about it.
think: Five years lets me build the business on a **police wage** first.
Going full time around **2029** is a sensible order.
do: Grow surveys to **two or three jobs** a month and bank the money.
Apply for the **drone unit** to get more flying hours.
**Leave the force** around 2029 to go full time.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like before a big match.
S3.quote: When robots arrive, I'd be selling and managing the robots, not flying the drone. Somebody has to own the kit and find the customers.
fieldNote: Five years lets Felix **sequence** his move sensibly.
He sees himself as an **owner of machines**, not a worker replaced by them.
Encourages housemates toward **self-reliance**, not union or state help.

steps.text: Grow weekend drone surveys to three jobs a month
Bank all survey income until three months are saved
Leave the force around 2029 for the drone business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with ambition. Start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks good for me. Ten years to build a business, get a few staff, buy proper kit. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and, if it works, owning the robots instead of being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the force for maybe five more years, get into the drone unit, and run the survey business at weekends. Every spare bit of money goes into better kit. Around 2031, I'd go full time and hire someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Money's still thin, but the direction feels right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm, but your savings are still under a month. Isn't that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, day to day. But in ten years it can change. I'm not worried about where things end up, I'm worried about the boiler at the house, and that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd keep from police work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The calm under pressure, and the way you learn to read a scene fast. Those are worth more than any drone. I'd want those in whoever I hire.

say: Ten years is a **gift** for anyone with ambition.
My advice to anyone is simple: **start something** now.
think: By 2039 I'd be **owning the robots** instead of being replaced by them.
Ten years is enough to build a business, hire **staff** and buy kit.
do: Stay in the force **five more years** and join the drone unit.
Put every spare penny into **better drone kit**.
Go **full time** around 2031 and hire someone.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with thin money but a direction that feels right.
S4.quote: I'm not worried about where things end up, I'm worried about the boiler at the house, and that's normal.
fieldNote: With a decade, Felix sees the change as **good for him**.
He separates **daily money worry** from his view of the future.
He would carry police **calm under pressure** into his own firm.

steps.text: Join the force's drone unit and stay five more years
Put spare money into better drone kit each year
Run the survey business at weekends until 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything before my edge disappears, and I've got nothing in the bank. What would help is less red tape for new businesses, cheaper finance for kit, and the force letting officers do side work without months of forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about risk. People my age get told to play it safe, but safe jobs are the ones going first. I'd rather fail at something I built than be laid off from something I didn't.

headlineQuote: I'd rather fail at something I built than be laid off from something I didn't.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old response officer** and trained drone pilot at Riverside station.
He spent his savings on a **commercial drone licence** and kit, leaving under a month in the bank.
He uses AI daily and sees change as an **opportunity**, not a threat.
Under fast AGI he'd **leave the force** quickly to run drone services, despite real fear.
With a decade, he plans to **own the robots** rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which removes his edge before he can build a business.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape**, cheaper finance for kit and easier permission for officers' side work.
